title: LServe: Efficient Long-sequence LLM Serving with Unified Sparse Attention
technique: unified block-sparse attention: static streaming heads + dynamic hierarchical KV page selection with reusable selector, plus KV quantization

optimized_metrics.evidence: For the prefilling stage, we use time-to-first-token (TTFT) as a key metric
while for the decoding stage, we emphasize minimizing the per-token generation latency
Our primary focus is on serving throughput.
LServe accelerates LLM prefilling by up to 2.9x and decoding by 1.3-2.1x over vLLM, maintaining long-context accuracy

headline_claim.text: On average, LServe accelerates LLM prefilling by up to 2.9x and decoding by 1.3-2.1x over vLLM, maintaining long-context accuracy.

reported_metrics.where: Tables 2-4, Fig 9 (LongBench, NIAH, RULER, AIME, MATH500)

metric_definitions.definition_quote: Our primary focus is on serving throughput. For the prefilling stage, we use time-to-first-token (TTFT) as a key metric, while for the decoding stage, we emphasize minimizing the per-token generation latency.
metric_definitions.notes: throughput stated as primary focus but plotted as relative speed normalized to LServe (Fig 10); no formal throughput units or percentiles; TTFT here is single-request prefill latency (no queueing)

load_regime: input-length sweep (32K-256K), single request / fixed batch; no arrival process
tradeoff_acknowledged: LServe-8192 only up to 6% slower than dense in some long-context tasks; small accuracy deviations
workloads: LongBench, NIAH, RULER, AIME2024, MATH500; synthetic length sweeps
extractor_notes: Paper says primary focus is serving throughput, but the evaluated quantities are prefill latency (TTFT) and decode per-step latency/speedup; effectively kernel-level latency. Genuinely ambiguous whether throughput or latency is the objective.
